Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)

through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

A simple terminal UI for git commands. ## Description Lazygit is a terminal UI for git commands that makes working with git easier and more intuitive. Instead of typing complex git commands, you can use a simple visual interface to perform common git operations. ## Features ### Stage individual lines Press space on the selected line to stage it, or press `v` to start selecting a range of lines. You can also press `a` to select the entirety of the current hunk. ### Interactive Rebase Press `i` to start an interactive rebase. Then squash (`s`), fixup (`f`), drop (`d`), edit (`e`), move up (`ctrl+k`) or move down (`ctrl+j`) any of TODO commits, before continuing the rebase by bringing up the rebase options menu with `m` and then selecting `continue`. ### Cherry-pick Press `shift+c` on a commit to copy it and press `shift+v` to paste (cherry-pick) it. ### Bisect Press `b` in the commits view to mark a commit as good/bad in order to begin a git bisect. ### Nuke the working tree For when you really want to just get rid of anything that shows up when you run `git status`, press `shift+d` to bring up the reset options menu and then select the 'nuke' option. ### Amend an old commit Pressing `shift+a` on any commit will amend that commit with the currently staged changes (running an interactive rebase in the background). ### Filter You can filter a view with `/`. For example, filter down the branches view and then hit `enter` to view its commits. ### Worktrees You can create worktrees to have multiple branches going at once without the need for stashing or creating WIP commits when switching between them. Press `w` in the branches view to create a worktree from the selected branch and switch to it. ### Undo Lazygit provides powerful undo capabilities. See the documentation for details. ### Commit graph Lazygit displays a visual commit graph showing the relationship between commits. ## Installation Lazygit is available through various package managers: ### Binary Releases Download pre-built binaries from the releases page. ### Homebrew (macOS and Linux) ```sh brew install lazygit ``` ### MacPorts (macOS) ```sh sudo port install lazygit ``` ### Scoop (Windows) ```sh scoop install lazygit ``` ### Chocolatey (Windows) ```sh choco install lazygit ``` ### Winget (Windows) ```sh winget install -e --id=JesseDuffield.lazygit ``` ### Arch Linux ```sh sudo pacman -S lazygit ``` ### Fedora / CentOS Stream ```sh sudo dnf install lazygit ``` ### Debian and Ubuntu ```sh sudo apt install lazygit ``` ### NixOS ```sh nix-env -iA nixpkgs.lazygit ``` ### FreeBSD ```sh pkg install lazygit ``` ### Conda ```sh conda install -c conda-forge lazygit ``` And many other package managers. Check your system's package manager for availability. ## Usage Call `lazygit` in your terminal inside a git repository: ```sh $ lazygit ``` You can also add an alias for convenience: ```sh echo "alias lg='lazygit'" >> ~/.zshrc ``` ### Changing Directory On Exit If you change repos in lazygit and want your shell to change directory into that repo on exiting lazygit, add this to your `~/.zshrc` (or other rc file): ```sh lg() { export LAZYGIT_NEW_DIR_FILE=~/.lazygit/newdir lazygit "$@" if [ -f $LAZYGIT_NEW_DIR_FILE ]; then cd "$(cat $LAZYGIT_NEW_DIR_FILE)" rm -f $LAZYGIT_NEW_DIR_FILE > /dev/null fi } ``` Then `source ~/.zshrc` and from now on when you call `lg` and exit you'll switch directories to whatever you were in inside lazygit. To override this behaviour you can exit using `shift+Q` rather than just `q`. ## Configuration ### Config File Location Default path for the config file: - Linux: `~/.config/lazygit/config.yml` - MacOS: `~/Library/Application Support/lazygit/config.yml` - Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\lazygit\config.yml` You can create repo-specific config files in `/.git/lazygit.yml`. Settings in these files override settings in the global config file. ### Keybindings Lazygit provides extensive keyboard shortcuts for all operations. {"command":"cd /workspace
rm -rf /home/agent/.local/state/lazygit/development.log

# Let's test more thoroughly the help annotation logic, by enumerating combinations and diffing with base help
./executable --help 2>&1 > /tmp/base.txt
# For each boolean flag alone with --help, see which line gets annotation
for flag in "--version" "-v" "--config" "-c" "--print-config-dir" "-cd" "--logs" "-l" "--debug" "-d" "--profile"; do
  ./executable $flag --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
  echo "=== $flag --help ==="
  diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"
  echo
done

echo "=== multiple flags ==="
./executable --version --config --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

./executable --version --config --print-config-dir --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

./executable --version --config --print-config-dir --logs --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

./executable --version --config --print-config-dir --logs --debug --profile --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

# Also test short flags combined?
echo "=== short flags ==="
./executable -v -c --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

# It appears that when a boolean flag is present, its line in help output gets " (default: false)" appended, except for flags that already have a default? Actually all bool flags are false by default.

# Let's also check if help flag itself gets annotation? It shouldn't.
./executable --help --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

echo "=== check -h short help annotation ==="
./executable -h 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"
./executable -h --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"
./executable -h -v --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
diff -u /tmp/base.txt /tmp/out.txt | grep "^+" | grep -v "^+++"

echo "=== what about string flags with help? Does string flags get default annotation? ==="
./executable --path /tmp --help 2>&1 > /tmp/out.txt
